title: A random number from a spinning wheel can sway your next guess
body: In a classic study, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman spun a wheel rigged to stop on either 10 or 65, then asked people what percentage of United Nations members were African countries. Those who saw 10 guessed about 25%, while those who saw 65 guessed about 45%. An obviously irrelevant number became a starting point, and people adjusted away from it too little. This anchoring effect has since held up well in large replication projects.

slides.clue: The bias in which an irrelevant starting number drags your estimate toward it
slides.detail: Like a ship’s anchor, the first number holds your guess near one spot, and people adjust away from it too little.
